svg.aria-label: Diagram: the Shared VPC shape where a host project owns the network and service projects attach to it at project level, with no nesting because a project cannot be both and a service project attaches to exactly one host; the two sharing scopes where sharing all subnets silently includes every future subnet and network; the four administrative roles and the split where network admin covers everything except firewall rules and SSL certificates which belong to security admin; why attaching a project migrates nothing because existing instances cannot be reconfigured onto a shared network; the organization policy constraints that are prospective only and never affect existing attachments or resources; and the billing model that attributes resources to the service project except VPN egress which lands on the host project regardless of which service project sent it
svg.title: Shared VPC: one host project owns the network, attachment grants nothing retroactively, and VPN egress bills the wrong cost centre
svg.text: One project owns the network. The others borrow subnets from it, and own their own VMs.
The model is strictly two levels deep, and attaching a project changes nothing that exists.
The shape, and why it cannot nest
A HOST PROJECT holds the Shared VPC networks. SERVICE PROJECTS attach to it, and their
eligible resources use its subnets. Attachments are at the PROJECT level.
A project CANNOT BE BOTH, so a service project cannot be a host to further service
projects. And a service project attaches to EXACTLY ONE host — a limit that cannot be raised.
Same organization only. Up to 100 host projects per organization. Legacy networks excluded.
Two sharing scopes, and one of them keeps growing
SHARE ALL SUBNETS: any new subnet created later, INCLUDING SUBNETS IN NEW NETWORKS,
is also shared. Project-level networkUser does the same for future networks.
SHARE INDIVIDUALLY: only the named subnets, until you change the list by hand.
So the docs tell you to RE-REVIEW the networkUser bindings each time you add a subnet.
Four roles, and the split that matters
ORGANIZATION ADMIN nominates Shared VPC Admins. SHARED VPC ADMIN is compute.xpnAdmin
plus Project IAM Admin, at organization or folder scope, and enables and attaches projects.
SERVICE PROJECT ADMIN is compute.networkUser on the host project or on chosen subnets.
NETWORK ADMIN has full control of all network resources EXCEPT firewall rules and SSL
certificates — those belong to SECURITY ADMIN. Routing and filtering are separate jobs.
Attaching a project migrates nothing, and the policies are prospective
Existing resources DO NOT automatically use the shared network. An existing instance
CANNOT BE RECONFIGURED onto it — a new one must be created. Same for private zones.
The two org policy constraints restrict only NEW attachments and NEW VMs and load
balancers. Existing attachments remain intact; existing resources keep operating.
A constraint is therefore a gate on growth, never an audit of what is already there.
Billing follows the resource — except where it does not
A resource bills to ITS SERVICE PROJECT even though it uses the host’s network, at the same
rates as if it lived in the host. That is what makes service projects usable as cost centres.
BUT VPN egress bills the project holding the VPN GATEWAY — usually the host — REGARDLESS
OF WHICH SERVICE PROJECT SENT IT. Interconnect egress bills whoever owns the attachment.
So the one path out of your network defeats the cost allocation the model exists to give you.
Two naming details worth knowing: the API calls this XPN, which is why the role is
compute.xpnAdmin; and internal DNS names use the SERVICE project’s project ID even though
they resolve to internal addresses in the host project’s subnets.
